La Tapisserie de la Reine Mathilde E41: Appellation French name occasionally usedE55: Type "The Tapestry of Queen Matilda". The name carries the French legend that the work was commissioned and created by Queen Matilda and her ladies-in-waiting; the article treats that legend as superseded.
An embroidered cloth nearly 70 metres long and 50 centimetres tall depicting the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, led by William, Duke of Normandy, challenging Harold II, King of England, and culminating in the Battle of Hastings. It consists of 58 scenes, all with Medieval Latin tituli, embroidered on linen with coloured woollen yarns. StatementE55: Type
Embroidered in crewel (wool yarn) on a tabby-woven linen ground 68.38 metres long and 0.5 metres wide, using two methods of stitching: outline or stem stitch for lettering and the outlines of figures, and couching or laid work for filling in figures. The background is not embroidered, providing a large, clear field of cloth which allows the figures and decorative elements to stand out. The design involved a broad central zone with narrow decorative borders top and bottom. The main yarn colours are terracotta or russet, blue-green, dull gold, olive green, and blue, with small amounts of dark blue or black and sage green; later repairs are worked in light yellow, orange, and light greens. Laid yarns are couched in place with yarn of the same or contrasting colour. DescriptionE55: Type

BT Classification as a tapestry (conventional) E17: Type Assignment tapestryE55: Type Conventional usage, not the assertion of this record. In common with other embroidered hangings of the early medieval period the piece is conventionally referred to as a "tapestry", although the designs are embroidered rather than woven in a tapestry weave, so it does not meet narrower definitions of a tapestry. It does meet the broader OED definition: "A textile fabric decorated with designs of ornament or pictorial subjects, painted, embroidered, or woven in colours, used for wall hangings, curtains, covers for seats". 9E60: Number The nine linen panels of the Bayeux Tapestry E22: Human-Made Object Nine linen panels, between fourteen and three metres in length, were sewn together after each was embroidered and the joins were disguised with subsequent embroidery. At the first join (end of scene 13) the borders do not line up properly but the technique was improved so that the later joins are practically invisible. The article does not identify the individual panels, so they are recorded here as one collective part rather than nine.

A Comprehensive Survey, London: Phaidon, 1957, revised 1965E31: Document Scholarly analysis in the 20th century concluded it was probably commissioned by William's half-brother, Bishop Odo of Bayeux. The article treats this as the leading view: "It is likely that it was commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother, and made for him in England in the 1070s." The reasons given are: three of the bishop's followers mentioned in the Domesday Book appear on the tapestry; it was found in Bayeux Cathedral, built by Odo; and it may have been commissioned at the same time as the cathedral's construction in the 1070s, possibly completed by 1077 in time for display at the cathedral's dedication. Christopher Norton, "Viewing the Bayeux Tapestry, Now and Then", Journal of the British Archaeological Association 172(1), 2019, pp. 52-89E31: Document Norton reviewed the various measurements of the length of the tapestry and of its nine individual linen panels and attempted to estimate the size and architectural design of the 11th-century Bayeux Cathedral. He considers the tapestry would have fitted well if hung along the south, west, and north arcades of the nave, and that the scenes can be correlated with the positions of the arcade bays in a dramatically satisfying way. He concludes that the tapestry was definitely designed to be hung in Bayeux Cathedral specifically, that it was designed to appeal to a Norman audience, and that it was probably designed for Bishop Odo.

"In 1729, the hanging was rediscovered by scholars at a time when it was being displayed annually in Bayeux Cathedral." In 1724 Antoine Lancelot had sent a report to the Academie Royale des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres about a sketch he had received of a work concerning William the Conqueror; he had no idea where or what the original was, although he suggested it could have been a tapestry, and despite further enquiries he discovered no more. The Benedictine scholar Bernard de Montfaucon made more successful investigations and found that the sketch was of a small portion of a tapestry preserved at Bayeux Cathedral. The object was never lost, buried or excavated: it was in continuous ecclesiastical custody and was being displayed annually. What was rediscovered was its identity and significance, by the scholarly community. S19 Encounter Event is used because its scope note covers knowledge of an object that "may be new to the group of people the actor belongs to. In that case, we would talk about discovery"; the archaeological reading of the class, about matter surrounding an object in situ, does not apply here. Two further transfers were ordered or attempted and did not take place, and the CIDOC CRM offers no way to record an intended transfer that did not occur, so they are recorded here as text. On 18 August 1944, three days before the Wehrmacht withdrew from Paris, Himmler sent a message, intercepted by Bletchley Park, ordering the tapestry to be taken to "a place of safety", thought to be Berlin. It was only on 22 August that the SS attempted to take possession of the tapestry, by which time the Louvre was again in French hands. Heinrich Himmler had coveted the work, regarding it as "important for our glorious and cultured Germanic history". "The tapestry arrived at the British Museum on 10 July 2026." It returned to England for the first time in possibly over 900 years. The loan was announced by President Emmanuel Macron in 2018 and again in July 2025; an initial exhibition date at the British Museum in 2022 was announced but did not materialise. The 2025 announcement set the loan for September 2026 to June 2027 in exchange for items from the Sutton Hoo site, the Lewis chessmen or the Battersea Shield being loaned to museums in Rouen and Caen. The exhibition is scheduled to run from 10 September 2026 to 11 July 2027. The UK government announced in December 2025 that the UK would be liable for covering up to 800 million pounds in potential damage during the loan. French art historian Didier Rykner launched a petition to block the loan, claiming that transporting the tapestry could damage its fabric; as of August 2025 over 40,000 people had signed it. Recorded here as a challenge to the transfer, not as reception.

In a series of pictures supported by a written commentary, the tapestry tells the story of the events of 1064-1066 culminating in the Battle of Hastings. The two main protagonists are Harold Godwinson, recently crowned King of England, leading the Anglo-Saxon English, and William, Duke of Normandy, leading a mainly Norman army. Events take place in a long series of scenes which are generally separated by highly stylised trees; the trees are not placed consistently, and the greatest scene shift, between Harold's audience with Edward after his return to England and Edward's burial scene, is not marked in any way at all. The central zone of the Bayeux Tapestry E36: Visual Item The central zone contains most of the action, which sometimes overflows into the borders either for dramatic effect or because depictions would otherwise be very cramped, for example at Edward's death scene. The tituli are normally in the central zone but occasionally use the top border.
The upper border of the Bayeux Tapestry E36: Visual Item A narrow decorative border. Occasionally carries tituli. Halley's Comet appears here at scene 32.
The lower border of the Bayeux Tapestry E36: Visual Item A narrow decorative border. It carries the fleet of ghost-like ships that hints at the coming invasion, and nude figures, some of corpses from battle, others of a ribald nature.
The borders are mostly purely decorative and only sometimes does the decoration complement the action in the central zone. The decoration consists of birds, beasts, fish and scenes from fables, agriculture, and hunting. There are frequent oblique bands separating the vignettes. There are nude figures, some of corpses from battle, others of a ribald nature. The border decoration is recorded collectively, as the article describes it, rather than vignette by vignette. The knights carry shields but show no system of hereditary coats of arms. The warriors are depicted fighting with bare hands, while other sources indicate the general use of gloves in battle and hunt.
The Norman Conquest of England, 1066 E7: Activity 1064-1066 E52: Time-Span 1064/1066E61: Time Primitive
The tapestry depicts the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, led by William, Duke of Normandy, challenging Harold II, King of England, and culminating in the Battle of Hastings. It tells the story from the point of view of the conquering Normans.
The Battle of Hastings, 14 October 1066 E7: Activity 14 October 1066E52: Time-Span 1066-10-14E61: Time Primitive
The battle was fought less than three weeks after the Battle of Stamford Bridge but the tapestry does not provide this context. The English fight on foot behind a shield wall, whilst the Normans are on horses. Two fallen knights are named as Leofwine and Gyrth, Harold's brothers, but both armies are shown fighting bravely.
The appearance of Halley's Comet, 1066 E5: Event Scene 32, in the upper border: a star with a streaming tail, now known to be Halley's Comet. This is the first known picture of this comet. A comet was believed to be a bad omen at this time, and Halley's Comet would have first appeared in 1066 around 24 April, nearly four months after Harold's coronation.
The death of Edward the Confessor, 5 January 1066 E69: Death Scenes 26-27. The tapestry strongly suggests that, on his deathbed, Edward bequeaths the crown to Harold. The death scene is one where the action overflows into the borders.
The coronation of Harold Godwinson, 6 January 1066 E7: Activity Scene 31. What is probably the coronation ceremony is attended by Stigand, whose position as Archbishop of Canterbury was controversial. Stigand is performing a liturgical function, possibly not the crowning itself. The tapestry labels the celebrant "Stigant Archieps" although by that time he had been excommunicated by the papacy, who considered his appointment unlawful.
The death of Harold Godwinson, 14 October 1066 E69: Death Scene 57, with the legend "(Hic) Harold rex interfectus est" ("[Here] King Harold was killed"). The identification of Harold in this vignette is disputed: the name "Harold" appears above a number of knights, one character appears with an arrow shot in his head under the name "Harold" while another is slain by a sword underneath the words "was slain". It was common medieval iconography that a perjurer was to die with a weapon through the eye; the tapestry might therefore be said to emphasise William's rightful claim by depicting Harold as an oath breaker.
Harold's oath on saintly relics E7: Activity Scene 23. William gives Harold arms and armour, possibly knighting him, and Harold takes an oath on saintly relics. Although the writing on the tapestry explicitly states an oath is taken there is no clue as to what is being promised. Norman sources claim that the English succession was being pledged to William; English sources give varied accounts.
The scene of the cleric and Aelfgyva E5: Event A panel with what appears to be a clergyman touching or possibly striking a woman's face, captioned "ubi unus clericus et AElfgyva" ("where a certain cleric and AElfgyva"). No one knows the significance of this scene or its caption. AElfgyva is the Latinised spelling of AElfgifu, a popular Anglo-Saxon woman's name; the use of the grapheme AE shows familiarity with English spelling. Two naked male figures appear in the border below, the one directly below the figure in a pose mirroring that of the cleric. Modelled as an E5 Event of unspecified nature because the article states that what is depicted is unknown.
AElfgifu (AElfgyva)E21: Person "a woman of uncertain identity". Candidates the article canvasses: Harold's younger sister AElfgifu, spelt Alveva in the Domesday Book of 1086, possibly promised or betrothed to William but who died c. 1066; and AElfgifu of Northampton, mother of Sweyn Knutsson and Harold Harefoot.

Scenes the article discusses individually and that are recorded above or here: scene 1, Edward the Confessor sending Harold to Normandy; scene 7, Harold taken prisoner by Guy, Count of Ponthieu; scene 17, the army mired in quicksand outside Mont Saint-Michel and Harold saving two Norman soldiers; scene 20, Conan's surrender at Dinan after William's army chases him from Dol de Bretagne to Rennes; scene 23, the oath; scene 25, Harold's return and Edward's apparent remonstration; scenes 26-27, Edward's death and burial; scene 31, the coronation; scenes 32-33, the comet and the ghost ships; scene 35, the ordering of the fleet; scene 43, William's men finding food and a meal being cooked; scene 47, a house burnt by two soldiers, with a woman holding her boy's hand as she asks for humanity; scene 51, William's speech to prepare his army; scene 54, Odo rallying the troops; scene 57, Harold's death; scene 58, the final remaining scene, showing unarmoured English troops fleeing the battlefield. The remaining scenes of the 58 are not enumerated: the depicted narrative is the bulk of the article and modelling it scene by scene would sit at a finer grain than the rest of this record. BT Attribution 18: the tapestry as an apologia for the Norman Conquest E13: Attribute Assignment overall interpretationE55: Type The tapestry was probably commissioned by the House of Normandy and essentially depicts a Norman viewpoint. However, Harold is shown as brave, and his soldiers are not belittled. The fact that the narrative extensively covers Harold's activities in Normandy in 1064 indicates that the intention was to show a strong relationship between that expedition and the Norman Conquest starting two years later. It is for this reason that the tapestry is generally seen by modern scholars as an apologia for the Norman Conquest.

The tituli of the Bayeux Tapestry E34: Inscription Medieval LatinE56: Language Bayeux TapestryE22: Human-Made Object Tituli are included in many scenes to explain the event being depicted and point out names of specific people and places. The text is in Latin but at times the style of words and spelling shows an English influence. A dark blue wool, almost black, is mostly used, but towards the end of the tapestry other colours are used, sometimes for each word and other times for each letter. The tituli are normally in the central zone but occasionally use the top border. Their awkward placing is not due to their being added later: the woollen threads behind the linen show that all aspects were embroidered together at a session. The complete text is not reproduced here; the article devolves it to a separate page. Individual tituli quoted by the article: "Stigant Archieps"; "ubi unus clericus et AElfgyva"; "(Hic) Harold rex interfectus est"; "interfectus est"; and the spurious final "Et fuga verterunt Angli". Lucien Musset, The Bayeux Tapestry, Boydell Press, 2005E31: Document

The missing final section of the Bayeux Tapestry E22: Human-Made Object The end of the tapestry has been missing from time immemorial. At least two panels of the tapestry are missing, perhaps even another 6.4 m in total. No event is modelled for the loss: the article records no destruction, no removal and no date, only the absence, and asserting an E6 Destruction or an E80 Part Removal would be inventing a history. The three estimates of its length that the article carries are recorded below as alternative dimensions. This missing area may have depicted William's coronation as King of England. A poem by Baldric of Dol describes a tapestry on the walls of the personal apartments of Adela of Normandy which is very similar to the Bayeux depiction, and he describes the closing scene as the coronation of William in London. It is thought that the story contained only one additional scene.
